vignette:
He was twenty-eight when he met her, a woman with a laugh that filled the room and a temper that emptied it. At first, the bruises were easy to hide—a collarbone he said he’d hit on a cabinet door, a wrist he’d twisted playing volleyball. He believed her apologies, believed the promises that it would never happen again. The community center where he worked as a young organizer became his refuge: long hours canvassing, late-night meetings, any excuse to stay away. But the night she threw a ceramic vase at his head—the shards gouging his scalp, the blood pooling under his ear—he finally left. He never pressed charges. He told himself it was over.

Now he is fifty-four, a senior community organizer in a midsize city, married for sixteen years to a quiet, steady woman named Layla. Most people see a calm, deliberate man who listens carefully before speaking. They do not see that he has never fully left that apartment. The hypervigilance that served him as a young man—scanning a room for exits, reading the tilt of someone’s shoulders for sudden anger—has become a permanent filter. At work, he can advocate for tenants or lead a protest rally, but afterward, he needs an hour alone in his car, checking his rearview mirror over and over, convinced someone is following him. He has learned to schedule one-on-one meetings instead of group lunches; the noise and unpredictability of a crowded table trigger a rushing in his ears, a tightness in his chest that makes him fumble for the restroom.

The nightmares come three or four times a week. He sees her face, not as it was, but contorted, the vase arcing toward him in slow motion. He wakes gasping, sheets twisted, and Layla reaches for him in the dark. He cannot tell her what he saw—not because she wouldn’t understand, but because the shame of staying for so long is a weight he still cannot lift. He avoids any television show or news story about domestic violence. When a colleague mentions a training on intimate partner abuse, he says he has a conflict and leaves the room, his palms sweating.

Layla knows he was hurt before they met, but not the details. He has never shown her the scar beneath his hairline. At family gatherings, he positions himself so his back is to the wall, and he watches the door. He never raises his voice in an argument—never even disagrees firmly—because the sound of any raised voice, even Layla’s when she’s excited, sends a jolt of adrenaline through him. Once, at a community meeting, a man pounded the table in frustration. He excused himself, walked to the bathroom, and stood gripping the sink for ten minutes, waiting for his hands to stop shaking.

His PCL-5 score is seventy-six. He knows the number because after the intake he looked at it on the printed sheet, his eyes catching the sum before he folded it away. It means he is living inside a body that is always waiting for the next blow. He cannot remember a time when his shoulders were not hunched, when his stomach was not knotted. He tells himself that he is lucky—he has a good marriage, a meaningful job, his health. But luck does not stop him from flinching at sudden movement, or from checking his phone for texts from a number he blocked twenty-five years ago, just in case.

He came to therapy because Layla told him, gently, that he seemed “always somewhere else.” He did not argue. He is tired of carrying the apartment with him. He sits in the chair across from me, his hands folded in his lap, and describes that night in a voice so measured and flat that it sounds like a weather report. But his jaw is tight, and he has not blinked in a long time.
